introduction-running-on-empty.core: ISPs ran out of IPv4 addresses to give each customer. Carrier-grade NAT (NAT444) adds a second NAT layer inside the ISP: customer routers get private addresses from 100.64.0.0/10 and the ISP translates many customers onto a small pool of public IPs, often 10 to over 1,000 subscribers per address. It stretches IPv4 but breaks inbound connectivity, complicates logging and degrades some apps.

first_principles.problem: A new mobile carrier has 2 million subscribers and only 16,000 public IPv4 addresses.

analogy.title: A shared office building with one mailing address
analogy.story: Hundreds of companies share one street address; the mailroom sorts by suite number (port).
analogy.breaks: Mailrooms know every tenant; external parties can't distinguish CGN users.

check.q: What address range is reserved for CGNAT?

identifying-cgnat-rfc-6598.core: You're likely behind CGNAT if your router's WAN address is in 100.64.0.0/10 (or a private range) while websites report a different public IP, or if traceroute shows 100.64.x.x hops. RFC 6598 reserved that range so ISPs wouldn't collide with customers' own 10/8 and 192.168/16 LANs. It must never be routed on the public internet or used for internal enterprise networks.

first_principles.problem: Port forwarding configured on a home router does nothing, and the user doesn't know why.
truths: WAN IP vs observed public IP reveals NAT layers.

analogy.title: Realising your 'house number' is really a flat number
analogy.story: Letters to your flat number never arrive from outside because the building's street address is shared.
analogy.breaks: You can see the building; you can't see the CGN.

code.text:
# on router/WAN
ip -4 addr show wan | grep inet      # inet 100.72.14.9/10
curl -s https://ifconfig.me          # 203.0.113.77
# different → behind CGNAT

check.q: Why didn't ISPs just use 10.0.0.0/8 for CGNAT?
check.a: Customers already use 10/8 on their LANs; overlapping ranges would break routing, so RFC 6598 reserved a distinct shared range.

the-port-forwarding-problem.core: Port forwarding on your router maps an inbound public port to a LAN host, but under CGNAT your router has no public IP. Inbound connections hit the ISP's CGN, which has no mapping for unsolicited traffic and drops it. Self-hosted servers, remote access, cameras and game hosting stop working. Fixes need ISP cooperation, outbound tunnels or IPv6.

first_principles.problem: A small business can't reach its on-site NVR remotely after the ISP moved it to CGNAT.
truths: NAT allows replies, not unsolicited inbound.
Your router is not the outermost NAT.

analogy.title: A gated community with a single gate guard
analogy.story: You can leave and visitors you called can come back, but strangers asking for your house are turned away, and your own doorbell is behind the gate.
analogy.breaks: Guards can be asked nicely; CGNs need ISP config.

code.text:
cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:8080
# Your quick Tunnel: https://random-words.trycloudflare.com
# (connection initiated outbound → works through CGNAT)

check.q: Why do outbound tunnels work behind CGNAT?
check.a: The connection is initiated from inside, so the CGN creates a mapping and allows the return traffic that carries inbound requests.

p2p-and-gaming-strict-nat.core: Peer-to-peer apps (games, VoIP, WebRTC) need direct paths between peers behind NATs. STUN discovers each peer's public mapping, and hole punching sends simultaneous packets to open mappings. CGNs often use endpoint-dependent (symmetric) mapping and short timeouts, which defeats hole punching, so consoles show 'Strict NAT' and apps fall back to TURN relays, adding latency and cost.

first_principles.problem: Gamers behind CGNAT can't host lobbies and get high-latency relayed voice chat.
truths: Symmetric NAT changes ports per destination.
Relays always work but cost latency.

analogy.title: Two people in different gated estates trying to meet
analogy.story: If guards issue predictable visitor passes, they can arrange to meet at the gates; if passes change every time, they need a café in between (relay).
analogy.breaks: People can phone each other; peers need a signalling server first.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Call works via relay, with added latency.

code.text:
candidate: host  192.168.1.20:50000
candidate: srflx 203.0.113.77:61234   (from STUN)
candidate: relay 198.51.100.5:3478    (TURN)
# symmetric CGN → srflx fails, relay chosen

check.q: Why does symmetric NAT defeat hole punching?
check.a: It assigns a different external port per destination, so the mapping learned via STUN doesn't apply to the peer.

the-reputation-problem-the-noisy-neighbo.core: Under CGNAT hundreds of users share one public IP, so IP-based reputation and rate limiting punish everyone. One subscriber's spam, scraping or abuse gets the IP blacklisted, CAPTCHAs appear for all, and rate limits hit innocent neighbours. For services, blocking or throttling by IP is unreliable when IPs are shared. Combine it with account, device and behaviour signals.

first_principles.problem: A whole neighbourhood gets endless CAPTCHAs on a search engine because one user behind the same CGN IP runs a scraper.
truths: Abuse attribution needs ports and timestamps.
derivation: Log **source port + timestamp** for abuse reports.

analogy.title: One rowdy guest gets a whole hotel banned
analogy.story: The bar bans the hotel's address, so every guest is turned away.
analogy.breaks: Bars can check ID; services need non-IP identity signals.

example.title: Smarter rate limiting
flow: Bot signals: challenge only suspicious sessions

check.q: What extra information is needed to attribute abuse from a CGNAT IP?
check.a: The source port and precise timestamp, which the ISP can match against its CGN translation logs.

solutions-escaping-the-cage.core: Options to escape CGNAT limits: ask the ISP for a public or static IPv4 (often a paid add-on); use IPv6, which avoids NAT entirely; use outbound overlay networks (Tailscale, ZeroTier, Cloudflare Tunnel, ngrok) for remote access; rent a cheap VPS with a public IP and tunnel to it (WireGuard plus port forwarding); or use ISP-supported Port Control Protocol where available.

first_principles.problem: A home-lab user needs reliable remote SSH and a web dashboard from behind CGNAT.

analogy.title: Getting mail when your building has no letterbox
analogy.story: Rent a PO box elsewhere (VPS), use a courier who picks up from you (tunnel), or move to a building with letterboxes (IPv6).
analogy.breaks: PO boxes are cheap and static; relays add a dependency and latency.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Public 443 on VPS reaches home server through CGNAT.

code.text:
# on VPS (public IP 198.51.100.9), wg0 peer = home 10.8.0.2
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.8.0.2:443
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wg0 -j MASQUERADE
# home keeps WireGuard tunnel up (PersistentKeepalive = 25)

check.q: Why does the home side need PersistentKeepalive in a WireGuard relay setup?
check.a: To keep the CGN mapping alive so the VPS can always send traffic back down the tunnel.
